feedback: If the child predicts both plants will look the same because both are watered, point to the pale, floppy dark plant: 'The cupboard plant got water too — so why isn't it healthy? What did it miss out on?'

If the child says the plant just needs feeding, explain that plants are not fed like pets or people; the needs we are testing are light, water and a suitable temperature, so watering is not the same as feeding — save exactly how plants use these for later (KS2).
Reinforce: 'The one in the cupboard went pale and floppy because it had no light' — attribute the change to the single factor that was removed.
If the dark plant still looks green and standing after a day or two, keep observing: etiolation takes time, so don't judge it 'fine' early.
activities.intendedInsight: Light is a genuine growth need, not an optional extra — watering alone does not keep a plant healthy. Over days the dark plant goes pale, leggy and floppy while its watered twin in the light stays green and sturdy.
learnerActions: Start with two identical pots of young green cress (or bean) seedlings, keep both soils similarly moist, and put one on a bright windowsill and one in a dark cupboard.
Before waiting, write or say a prediction: how will each plant look after a week, and WHY?
Keep a growth diary: draw the same plant on day 1, 3, 5 and 7 to make the slow change visible.
After a week, describe the result and name which single need was missing for the cupboard plant.
activities.title: Windowsill vs cupboard: a real cress comparison
